rv.q: Tyler Ferguson navigates these human mountains and valleys, major torrents and tricky rivulets, with precision and even empathy; it’s a virtuosic performance and the audience, you should pardon the expression, eats it up.

“Some of the jokes could be sharper...it is often strangely polite...But Ferguson is an actor of such irrepressible amiability...Under Jason Moore’s direction, a few of the actorly shifts could occur more quickly and not all the personae have a gestural specificity to match the vocal one.
The amount of concentration required by Ferguson is impressive and director Jason Moore runs a tight ship.
Even so, his acting crackles with physical energy and comic life, and it won’t take long for you to shelve your doubts and buy into his performance.
The sustained enjoyment comes from the impressively controlled mayhem activated by Ferguson, under Jason Moore’s savvy direction.
Asking a play that is basically a clever stunt to support the weight of this more complex interpretation is asking for trouble, which here takes the form of a strange pall.
Lively as Mr. Ferguson is, and as frequently hilarious as “Fully Committed” can be, it feels shrunken in a Broadway theater.
But he shines as one character: Sam.
The actor's likability glazes his hamminess with sugar, and the play, while not very filling, can be enjoyed with few reservations.
So it feels bad to have to say this, but Ferguson, despite exhausting commitment to this demanding 80-minute comic showcase, is totally wrong for “Fully Committed.”

It’s always satisfying and fun and exciting to discover a brilliantly talented comedian with star quality -like Jesse Tyler Ferguson-who is himself fully committed to knocking himself out for our pleasure.

Backed by an affable and charismatic lead actor, Fully Committed is a well-rounded production that is fun and energetic, and—between the myriad of characters popping in and out of the story—has a message full of heart and sincerity.
This blissfully frenetic expedition takes things to a whole new level.
The fleet and funny 'Fully Committed' proves to be an ideal vehicle for Ferguson, letting him display his full range of comic skills.
Ferguson juggles all of these personalities rather deftly, making only a few fumbles.
And while it’s not cutting-edge cuisine, Ferguson makes sure it’s delicious.
There's still something for everyone on this menu, which makes Fully Committed the rare nutrition-free amuse-bouche that genuinely, unapologetically amuses.
Ferguson uses his performing skill and endearing personality to create a very engaging evening.

Fans of this restaurant-reservationist comedy will not be disappointed, and fans of “Modern Family” will be delighted to see Jesse Tyler Ferguson live on stage playing not one character but a few dozen.
Mr. Ferguson gives a more diverse and warm performance than Benjamin Walker.
Because Ferguson makes it fast and funny.
Without an expert mimic taking charge, Fully Committed is little more than pleasantly amusing with a sweet finish.
The actor is fully committed, yes, but the production isn't totally satisfying.
Still, it seems like a plate of hors d’oeuvres at a party: If the tray passes in front of you, you’ll probably eat one and enjoy it, but there’s no real reason to seek it out.
But I wonder whether there is a better choice of vehicle out there to deliver Ferguson’s talents to a Broadway audience.
By the end, it has become a whirling blur of silly voices and high-strung personalities.
But when you're chewing on dust, even a tour de force can't entirely compensate for a flavorless show.
If you want to laugh, you need to check this show out.
Thanks to a very strong performance and excellent production values all around, this is one completely fulfilling and satisfying experience.
Mr. Ferguson perfectly captures the pain, absurdity, and, strangely, the power of one consigned to such a position, in the vortex of this new reality.

Because the audience actually gets to know Sam, and if you've ever hustled to achieve something, be it a career — in acting or any other business — or a reservation at the hottest restaurant in town, you're likely to recognize a bit of yourself in more than one character by the end.
Unfortunately, most of the characters aren’t fleshed-out characters but voices Sam has to interact with on the telephone; from family, friends and bosses to lame customers with astounding demands.
It is a one-man show and that man, Modern Family’s Emmy-nominated Jesse Tyler Ferguson, plays 40 characters with near-pitch perfection.

Ferguson is likable and skillful but, with the characters being so cartoonish and the need to differentiate them requiring such obvious choices, his enterprise becomes more a technical than an artistic feat.
At Broadway prices ($$) and a stage about 8x larger than what the show should be presented on, I found little to enjoy and many-a-glance at my watch to check when 90 minutes would finally be up.

cn.t: Ferguson delivers an energetic tour de force playing 40+ characters in this one-man restaurant comedy, though critics are divided on whether his talents suit the over-the-top material and if the 90s satire still resonates today.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
